name: Biology (PhD)

rules.name: Requirements Overview
rules.desc:
All students must be enrolled in exactly ten units during autumn, winter, spring, and summer quarters until reaching Terminal Graduate Registration (TGR) status. Satisfactory completion of each year’s general and track-specific requirements listed below is required for satisfactory progress toward the degree. Students not making satisfactory degree progress are subject to departmental academic review and/or dismissal.
Note: A student’s Advising Committee and the Graduate Studies Committee Chair consider written petitions for exemptions to requirements. Approval is contingent on special circumstances and is not routinely granted.

• First-year advising
Entering CMOB students will meet with the DGS in the first quarter to discuss rotations and year 1 recommendations. In the first quarter, students in the Eco/Evo subplan must also meet with their first-year advising committee. The committee reviews the student's previous academic work and current goals and advises the student on a program of Stanford courses, some of which may be required and others recommended. All students must complete the core curriculum listed below under Subplan Specific Requirements.

• Seminars
Graduate seminars devoted to current literature and research in particular fields of biology are an essential means of attaining professional perspective and competence. Seminars are presented under individual course listings or are announced by various research groups.
During the first year of study, graduate students must attend seminars. For CMOB, this includes enrolling in BIO 301 and attending the corresponding department seminar series. For Eco/Evo, this includes enrolling in and attending BIO 302/303/304 in Autumn, Winter, and Spring of the first year, making one formal seminar presentation, and writing a research paper, both of which must be evaluated by a minimum of two Biology faculty members.

• Committee meetings
Students must meet regularly with their advising committees. These meetings will be annual or semi-annual for advanced students in year 5+.

• Individual Development Plan meetings
Students must meet once a year with their advisor by August 1 of that academic year.

• Publishable manuscript
Over the course of the PhD, each student must complete one publishable manuscript (paper) for which they are the major contributor and first author. This work should be of recognized high quality by the primary research advisor and thesis committee and be published or being prepared for publication in a reputable journal. This is to be completed by the time of graduation. In some fields, students should have multiple first-authored research papers, which serve as thesis chapters. Decisions about how much primary research constitutes a PhD dissertation are made in consultation between the advisor, faculty committee, and PhD student
Subplan Specific Requirements
In addition to the general requirements listed above, students must complete requirements within their Subplan (see Subplan Options Categories below). The advising committee and the graduate studies committee chair consider written petitions for exemptions to core curriculum and lab rotation requirements. Approval is contingent upon special circumstances and is not routinely granted.

rules.name: One publishable first-author manuscript by graduation
Regular advising committee meetings and an annual Individual Development Plan meeting
Required Enrollment Course
rules.desc: BIO 290 is to be taken concurrently with each quarter of required teaching. BIO 296 is to be taken concurrently with the first quarter of required teaching. Enrollment should be commensurate with the course for which they are teaching. Please see the handbook on the program requirement page for enrollment guidelines.

rules.name: Two quarters of Mentored Teaching Experience by Autumn of the third year
rules.desc:
Teaching experience and training are part of the graduate curriculum. Each student must complete 2 quarters of a Mentored Teaching Experience (MTE) by Autumn Quarter of the third year. At least one course at the introductory/foundational level (BIO 40s and 80s level courses; BIOS and summer session courses do not fulfill this requirement). Note: Students with a primary working location of Hopkins Marine Station, will complete at least one MTE requirement on campus during the first year. Any remaining teaching requirements can be met at Hopkins.

• A second course that can be either an introductory/foundational course or another biology or Hopkins Marine Station course, based on departmental needs.
Teaching is core to the academic and professional training of doctoral students in our program. All students are required to complete 2 quarters of teaching experience in Biology courses by Autumn of their third year in the program regardless of their financial support. The opportunities to gain teaching experience and training in specific courses are assigned using the departmental matching system during the Spring and Summer quarters before the next academic year.

rules.name: Advancement to Candidacy

children.name: Oral qualifying exam with advisor and faculty committee
Advisor chosen by end of year 1, candidacy by end of year 2

rules.desc:
Admission to candidacy is a prospective judgement by the faculty of a student’s potential to successfully complete the requirements of the degree program. Students are expected to complete qualifying procedures and apply for candidacy by the end of their second year in the program. Qualifying procedures include required coursework, research rotations, identification of an advisor by the end of the first year of the program, and successful completion of an oral qualifying exam with their advisor and faculty committee, in which they present an overview of their proposed dissertation research, respond to faculty questions, and discuss plans for their PhD. Failure to pass the qualifying exam as part of the admission to candidacy process could result in dismissal from the program. Additional details on qualifying procedures, including procedures for subsequent attempts to advance to candidacy in the event that the student does not successfully complete the qualifying exam, can be found in the Graduate Handbook .

Candidacy is valid for five years, subject to satisfactory academic progress. In the Department of Biology the procedure is outlined for each subplan in the Graduate Handbook

rules.name: Oral Exam
rules.desc: PhD students are required to give a ~50 minute research seminar summarizing their dissertation research, followed by 10 minutes of audience questions, which is attended by the committee and other department members and is open to the broader university and members of the public. Candidates and their committee then participate in a closed-door examination session in which candidates respond to further questions from the committee about the dissertation research. The timing of the oral exam is determined through joint consultations between the student, the primary research advisor, and all members of the thesis committee. Candidates are expected to provide each member of their PhD Oral Examination Committee (see below) a copy of their written dissertation at least 14 days before the scheduled oral defense date. This dissertation is expected to be in final or near-final form, pending any changes suggested by the student’s committee at the defense itself. The student should check in with the committee and incorporate any changes before or right after the exam.

rules.name: Dissertation
rules.desc: Along with completion of all Departmental and University requirements noted above, conferral of the PhD requires a written dissertation and successful completion of an oral exam. The written thesis is a document that expresses the contributions that the candidate has made (alone and/or in collaboration with others) to advancing knowledge. Typically, the written document contains several chapters, at minimum one chapter of introduction, one chapter of results, and one chapter of discussion or future directions. Additional chapters of results are common, and often correspond to distinct published or submitted manuscripts. Typically, the student is the first or co-first author on all their chapters. Regardless, the component of the work that was done by the candidate themself must be clearly identified and distinguishable from other aspects of the work. The evaluation of the Reading and Oral Committee should focus mainly on the component performed by the candidate. The specific roles of other major coauthors must be made clear in the thesis, and other presentations of the work.

rules.name: Non-Course Requirements

children.name: First-year paper approved by two Eco/Evo faculty by June 1
First-year oral research presentation in spring quarter

rules.desc:
• First-year paper: The paper should be read, commented upon, and agreed to as satisfactory by two Eco/Evo faculty by June 1. This can be satisfied in several ways involving new writing undertaken since entering the Stanford program. These may include:

• A new draft research manuscript (a previously published paper is unacceptable).

• Some other pieces of new writing, such as a review paper from a course or an initial literature review of a potential thesis topic. In this case, the paper should ordinarily be not less than ten double-spaced pages in standard-sized font and not more than ten single-spaced pages, plus references. It should be written in the style of a standard scientific paper.

• First-year presentation: First-year PhD students should give an oral research presentation in spring quarter with at least two faculty in attendance of the students’ choice. Additional details of this requirement can be found in the handbook. This may include any of the following:

• New research conducted in the first year of the PhD

• Plans for future research

• Literature review, background on a focal research topic, and proposed ideas

gpa: Biology does not require a minimum GPA other than the university required 3.0 to graduate with a graduate degree. Otherwise, students can opt to take courses CR/NC or S/NC.
grading: Students are not required to take any courses for a letter grade unless this is specifically noted in the course description.
transferPolicy: Students who completed graduate coursework at another institution are strongly encouraged to begin the process of transferring course units in winter quarter of their first year of doctoral study. The Directors of Graduate Studies for the student's respective subplan will evaluate transfer of units on a course-by-course basis. Graduate work accepted for transfer of residency does not automatically exempt a student from having to complete a course requirement for the degree.
reviewNotes: You pick the Cells, Molecules & Organisms or the Ecology/Evolution subplan, each with its own required courses (including its ethics course); CMOB adds two committee-approved courses you move in and the lab rotations, Eco/Evo the first-year paper and presentation. The audit checks BIO 290 for each of your two teaching quarters plus BIO 296, and 135 graduate units; no course has to be letter graded unless its description says so. The mentored teaching, the 3.0 GPA the university requires, committee meetings, the qualifying exam and candidacy, the oral exam, the dissertation and a first-author manuscript are checked by hand.
